🧙‍♂️🕷️ Lord of the Rings Session #5 - Frodo, Sam, Gollum, and the burden getting uglier
Book-club discussion - The Two Towers, Book IV.
Short summary
Last session stayed with the war side of The Two Towers.
This one goes back to the smaller, lonelier, more spiritually dangerous road.
Frodo. Sam. Gollum. Hunger. Swamps. Stairs. Trust. Pity. Exhaustion. The Ring getting heavier in a way that is not just physical.
This is the part of Tolkien where the adventure gets less grand and more intimate.
No armies to hide behind.
No heroic speeches to make the burden noble.
Just three figures moving through a poisoned landscape, and the uncomfortable question of what mercy costs when the person you pity might still betray you.
Reading for this session
The Two Towers - Book IV
From The Taming of Sméagol through The Choices of Master Samwise.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Is Gollum pitiable, dangerous, funny, tragic, or all of those at once?”
• “Does Frodo trust Gollum, use him, pity him, or need him?”
• “What makes Sam’s loyalty beautiful, and where does it become limited?”
• “Why does this section feel so much lonelier than the war chapters?”
• “What does Tolkien understand about addiction, burden, and divided selves?”
• “By the end, who understands the Ring best?”

How the evening will go
We’ll start with one question:
“What image from this section stayed with you?”
Then I’ll do a quick map reset and we’ll stay close to the scenes and choices.
Not lore-flexing.
Not pronunciation Olympics.
Not book-report voice.
A real Tolkien room.

VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.
Short summary
A lot of animated films ask you to choose a side.
Princess Mononoke does something more grown-up and more painful.
The forest is not innocent.
Industry is not simply evil.
The gods are terrifying.
The humans are desperate.
Everyone is wounded, hungry, proud, and half-right.
That is what makes this one of Miyazaki’s greatest films.
It is not a clean environmental fable. It is a war between ways of living, and the movie refuses to let anyone escape with a simple moral slogan.
This is the kind of film that deserves a room: beautiful, furious, mythic, political, and still hard to reduce.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Who is the film most sympathetic to, and does that change as you watch?”
• “Is coexistence actually possible here, or just the least impossible hope?”
• “What does the film understand about rage?”
• “Are the gods sacred, monstrous, or both?”
• “Does Lady Eboshi feel like a villain, a realist, a builder, or all three?”
• “Why does this movie make every easy answer feel dishonest?”

How the evening will go
We’ll meet at VIFF Centre before the screening, watch the film together, and whoever still has energy can stay for a short chat after.
This is a public VIFF screening, not a private Meetup event.
Please buy your own VIFF ticket while available.

events.description:
VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.
Short summary
It is very easy to be smug about Titanic.
Too famous.
Too big.
Too romantic.
Too many people have already cried over the door.
And yet.
The movie still works.
Partly because James Cameron understands spectacle. Partly because the romance is built with embarrassing confidence. Partly because the class story is not subtle but still lands. And partly because the whole film is really about memory: an old woman telling the story of the moment when her life split in two.
That is what makes this worth seeing with people.
Not ironic nostalgia.
Not “is there room on the door?” discourse for two hours.
A real conversation about sincerity, disaster, class, image, memory, and why some massive popular movies survive the jokes made about them.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Why does Titanic still work, even after all the parody?”
• “Is the romance simple, or exactly as simple as it needs to be?”
• “What does the film understand about class without being subtle about it?”
• “Does the spectacle deepen the emotion, or overpower it?”
• “Why does Rose’s memory frame matter so much?”
• “Is this a great film, a great popular film, or are those the same thing sometimes?”

How the evening will go
We’ll meet at VIFF Centre before the screening, watch the film together, and whoever still has energy can stay for a short chat after.
This is a long one. Assume it is your whole evening.
This is a public VIFF screening, not a private Meetup event.

VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.
Short summary
A lot of sci-fi ages into nostalgia.
The Matrix aged into an accusation.
Yes, it still has the coats, the bullet time, the sunglasses, the style. But what keeps it alive is the uglier thing underneath all that coolness: how much of your life is actually yours, and how much of it was handed to you so smoothly you stopped noticing?
Reality. Simulation. Bodies. Control. Choice. Comfort. The strange appeal of waking up, and the cost of not being able to go back to sleep.
This movie rewired how people talk about the world.
That is rare.
I want the real discussion, not internet red-pill sludge and not trivia about bullet time.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Would you really want the truth if it ruined your life?”
• “Is the Matrix mainly about freedom, control, or the desire to feel chosen?”
• “Was Cypher weak, honest, or saying something most people quietly feel?”
• “What part of the film stopped feeling futuristic and started feeling familiar?”
• “Do people want reality, or just a more flattering simulation?”
• “Once you wake up, are you free, or just trapped in a harsher system?”

How the evening will go
We’ll meet at VIFF Centre before the screening, watch the film together, and whoever wants can stay for a short post-film chat.
This is a public VIFF screening, not a private Meetup event.

events.description:
🧠⚠️ What should AI never be allowed to do for us? - Magnifica Humanitas

Interfaith / philosophy discussion - reading packet provided.

Short summary

Most AI debates get boring fast.
One side says: relax, it’s just a tool.
The other side says: panic, the machines are coming.
Too easy.
The better question is more uncomfortable:
What should AI never be allowed to do for us - even if it can do it efficiently?
Care for the lonely?
Teach children?
Choose who gets hired?
Write our apologies?
Mediate our friendships?
Decide who is risky, useful, visible, employable, or disposable?
That is where Magnifica Humanitas gets interesting.
The document is not saying “AI is evil.” It is also not saying “AI is neutral.” It asks whether we are building technologies that serve human beings, or systems that quietly redesign human beings into things that are easier to measure, rank, predict, manage, and discard.
That is a much better conversation than “AI good / AI bad.”

And to be very clear: this is not a Catholic-only event.
Religious people, spiritual people, agnostics, atheists, skeptics, tech people, non-tech people - all welcome.
The point is not conversion.
The point is not a sermon.
The point is not “the Vatican has all the answers.”
The point is asking whether secular tech culture is missing something important when it talks about human value only through productivity, convenience, intelligence, scale, and output.
Because maybe the most dangerous AI question is not:
“Can it think?”
Maybe it is:
“What kind of human beings are we becoming around it?”

A few questions already sitting in my head

\*“What is one human thing you would not want automated, even if a machine could do it efficiently?”
• “When does help become replacement?”
\*“Can AI imitate care so well that people stop expecting real care from each other?”
• “Is dignity just a religious word, or do non-religious people need it too?”
\*“What happens when a system treats you as a profile, risk score, output, or data trail instead of a person?”
• “What hidden suffering are we willing to ignore because digital life is convenient?”
\*“Does AI make us more creative, or more dependent on ready-made answers?”
• “What kind of weakness should be protected instead of upgraded away?”
\*“If AI reveals what a society loves, what does our society seem to love most: truth, profit, speed, control, comfort, or real human relationship?”

How the afternoon will go
We’ll start with one question:
“What is one way AI or algorithms already shape your daily life without asking permission?”
Then I’ll give a short reset on the reading packet:
Babel vs Jerusalem.
Dignity before efficiency.
AI as tool, not person.
Human beings as more than data, labour, output, or performance.
The common good.
Hidden costs.
What it might mean to stay human.
After that, we open the room.
Not a tech conference.
Not a church event.
Not culture-war sludge.
Not everyone turning their worldview into a billboard.
A serious room, but not a stiff one.
Come ready to disagree carefully.

Reading

events.description:
🏡💛 Won’t You Be My Neighbor? - can public kindness exist without becoming sentimental?
Documentary discussion - watch beforehand. Open spoilers.
Short summary
Kindness is one of those words that gets ruined by bad posters.
Be kind.
Choose kindness.
Kindness matters.
Fine. True. Also often completely dead on arrival.
That is why Won’t You Be My Neighbor? is worth a room.
Morgan Neville’s documentary about Fred Rogers is not interesting because it says “kindness is good.” That would be too easy. It is interesting because it shows a person trying to make gentleness serious in a culture that often treats gentleness as weakness, performance, or children’s programming.
And somehow that feels more radical now, not less.
This is a film about attention, childhood, television, public life, moral imagination, and whether a person can speak softly without becoming naïve.
I don’t want a sentimental nostalgia bath.
I want the harder conversation: what kind of public kindness is real, what kind is fake, and why modern life seems so bad at telling the difference.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Why does Fred Rogers feel so unusual now?”
• “Is his kindness simple, or is it actually disciplined?”
• “When does public goodness become sentimental performance?”
• “What did he understand about children that adults still avoid understanding about themselves?”
• “Can gentleness survive in a culture built around irony, speed, and attention-hunger?”
• “Did the documentary make you trust him more, or make you suspicious of your own cynicism?”
• “What would a grown-up version of neighbourliness look like now?”

How the morning will go
Come having watched the documentary beforehand.
We’ll start with one question:
“What moment felt least sentimental and most real?”
Then we’ll stay close to the film: Fred Rogers, television, childhood, public kindness, emotional honesty, religion without salesmanship, and why softness can sometimes be more demanding than toughness.
Open spoilers are fine.
Not therapy.
Not nostalgia worship.
Not everyone pretending they are nicer than they are.
A real conversation about whether kindness can still have moral weight without turning into wallpaper.

🤝📜 Cicero’s On Friendship - do we love our friends, or what they give us?
Short philosophy reading and discussion - read beforehand.
Short summary
Friendship is one of those words people use warmly and examine very badly.
We say “my friends.”
We say “community.”
We say “chosen family.”
We say “I’ve got people.”
But what do we actually mean?
Cicero’s On Friendship is old, but the question inside it is still awkwardly alive:
Do we love our friends for who they are, or for what they give us?
Comfort.
Status.
Access.
Validation.
Entertainment.
A version of ourselves we like being around.
Cicero is not writing a modern self-help essay about “finding your people.” He is asking what friendship is supposed to be when it is serious: loyalty, virtue, honesty, usefulness, affection, moral pressure, and whether a good friend should make your life easier or make you better.
That’s why this one feels worth a room.
Not networking.
Not sentimental friendship talk.
Not everyone pretending they are a perfect friend.
A real conversation about what friendship is, what it costs, and how much of what we call friendship is just mutual convenience with better branding.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Do we love our friends, or the version of ourselves we get to be around them?”
• “Can a friendship survive if it stops being useful?”
• “Should a real friend make you feel accepted, or tell you when you are becoming worse?”
• “Is loyalty still a virtue if your friend is wrong?”
• “What makes adult friendship so hard to maintain?”
• “Do we choose friends by character, chemistry, shared habits, or shared illusions?”
• “When does friendship become dependency?”
• “What would Cicero think of networking culture?”

How the morning will go
We’ll start with one question:
“What is one thing a real friend should be allowed to tell you?”
Then I’ll give a short reset on Cicero, the text, and the main argument.
After that, we stay close to the reading and let the bigger fight open up: friendship, virtue, usefulness, honesty, loyalty, and whether modern people have quietly lowered the standard for friendship because the real version asks too much.
Not philosophy-class stiffness.
Not therapy.
Not vague “community” language.
A real discussion.
Reading
Cicero - On Friendship
Also known as Laelius de Amicitia
Please read beforehand.

🐦⬜ The Story of a White Blackbird - what happens when being different becomes your entire identity?
Short story reading and discussion - read beforehand.
Short summary
Being different sounds glamorous until it becomes the only thing people can see.
Or worse: the only thing you know how to be.
Alfred de Musset’s The Story of a White Blackbird is a short, strange little fable from 1842 about difference, vanity, loneliness, recognition, and the trap of turning your outsider status into a whole personality.
That is why this one feels weirdly modern.
We live in a time where everyone is told to be unique, brandable, legible, interesting, exceptional, somehow unlike the others. But what happens when being different stops being freedom and becomes another cage?
The story is short, but the question is not.
Do we want to be understood, or admired?
Do we want belonging, or proof that we are special?
And what happens when identity becomes something we perform so well that we forget whether it was ever real?
Not a children’s fable night.
Not moral-of-the-story homework.
A real conversation about difference, ego, loneliness, and the ugly little hunger to be seen.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “When does being different become a gift, and when does it become a trap?”
• “Do people want to be loved for who they are, or recognized for what makes them unusual?”
• “Can outsider identity become its own kind of vanity?”
• “What happens when you build your whole self around not being like everyone else?”
• “Is it worse to be misunderstood, or to be understood only as ‘the different one’?”
• “How much of modern identity is self-knowledge, and how much is performance?”
• “What would this story look like now, in the age of personal branding and social media?”

How the afternoon will go
We’ll start with one question:
“What is one difference people praise in public but punish in real life?”
Then we’ll stay close to the story: the fable shape, the comedy, the loneliness, the desire to be seen, and the uneasy line between selfhood and self-display.
Not literature-class voice.
Not everyone pretending they are above vanity.
Not vague identity talk.
A real discussion.
Reading
Alfred de Musset - The Story of a White Blackbird

Please read it beforehand.

Summer is not always peaceful.
Sometimes it makes people more restless.
Heat. Late light. Open windows. City noise. Bodies outside. Everyone pretending they’re living fully because the weather is finally cooperating.
That’s the feeling for this one.
Poetry Night V is about heat, restlessness, the summer city, time passing too quickly, and that strange pressure to feel alive just because the days are longer.
This is not an open mic.
No performance voice required.
No school-style workshop.
No one dissecting your poem like it’s pinned to a lab tray.
Bring a poem, a stanza, a line, or just yourself. You can read something aloud if you want, or just listen and join the conversation.
The point is not to prove you “get poetry.”
The point is to notice what language does when ordinary speech starts feeling too flat for the season.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Why does summer make people feel more alive and more dissatisfied at the same time?”
• “What kind of restlessness only shows up when the weather is good?”
• “Does heat make people more honest, more dramatic, or just more tired?”
• “What line or image feels like a city summer to you?”
• “When does a poem feel true instead of just pretty?”
• “Is nostalgia worse in summer because everything looks like it should be meaningful?”
• “What does poetry catch that normal conversation usually misses?”

How the afternoon will go
We’ll start with a quick hello and a simple question:
“What line, poem, or image has been sitting with you lately?”
Then people can share a poem or short excerpt if they brought one.
Reading aloud is optional. Listening counts.
After each piece, we’ll talk about what it opens up: mood, language, memory, heat, city life, desire, boredom, time, whatever the room finds.
Not a critique circle.
Not a performance night.
Not literature-class stiffness.
A real conversation with language in the middle of it.

What we will discuss:

You can also bring a poem you want to talk about.
Bring a poem, stanza, line, or short excerpt if you want.
It can be old, modern, famous, obscure, funny, bitter, beautiful, annoying, whatever.
You can also come with nothing (i will bring a package to read)

events.description:
Biography / life-writing discussion - finish the full book beforehand.
Short summary
Some biographies turn people into saints.
Some turn them into villains.
The better ones make that impossible.
Walter Isaacson’s Steve Jobs is useful because Jobs is not easy to flatten. He is brilliant, difficult, obsessive, charismatic, cruel, visionary, controlling, childish, disciplined, impossible, and genuinely consequential.
That is exactly why this is worth a room.
Not because we need another “genius founder” worship session.
Not because everyone should pretend being awful is just the price of greatness.
Not because Apple nostalgia needs two hours of our lives.
I want the more interesting conversation:
What do we do with people who make beautiful things and damage people along the way?
How much bad behaviour gets excused when the products are good enough?
And why are modern people still so hungry for the myth of the singular genius who bends the world to his taste?
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “Is Jobs admirable, unbearable, or both?”
• “When does intensity become vision, and when is it just cruelty with better branding?”
• “Do great products make people forgive too much?”
• “Was Jobs a genius because he saw what people wanted, or because he forced people to want what he saw?”
• “What does the book reveal about taste as power?”
• “Can someone be a great builder and a bad model for how to live?”
• “Why do we keep wanting business figures to become moral heroes?”
• “What did the biography make you respect more, and what did it make harder to excuse?”

How the afternoon will go
Come having finished the full biography.
We’ll start with one question:
“What part of Jobs’ life made you most uncomfortable to admire?”
Then we’ll stay close to the book: the personality, the work, the relationships, the myth-making, the cruelty, the taste, the ambition, and the way Isaacson turns a business life into a study of character.
Full-book spoilers are expected.
Not startup worship.
Not anti-tech ranting.
Not everyone using Jobs as a personality test.
A real discussion about life-writing, power, creativity, and the cost of getting exactly what you want.

events.description:
Science fiction book club discussion - read beforehand.
Short summary
Some science fiction is loud because it wants to impress you.
Rendezvous with Rama is quieter than that.
A mysterious object enters the solar system. Humans go to look. And the real tension is not just “what is it?” but whether human beings are even capable of encountering something vast without immediately trying to explain, possess, classify, or shrink it down to our size.
That is what makes this one worth a room.
This is not sci-fi as lore dump.
Not space opera noise.
Not a fandom room where everyone tries to prove they know the most background detail.
A real discussion about awe, mystery, exploration, intelligence, humility, and what happens when the universe refuses to make itself emotionally convenient for us.
Some books give you answers.
This one is more interested in what happens when the answer stays bigger than the people asking.
A few questions already sitting in my head
• “What does the book do with mystery that modern sci-fi often ruins by over-explaining?”
• “Is Rama terrifying, beautiful, indifferent, or all of those at once?”
• “Do the human characters feel small in a good way, or almost too small?”
• “What would actually count as intelligence if it did not care about communicating with us?”
• “Does exploration require humility, or does it always carry some arrogance?”
• “Is the book emotionally cold, or is that part of its power?”
• “What is more unsettling: finding meaning, or finding something that does not need us at all?”

How the morning will go
Come having read the book beforehand.
We’ll start with one question:
“What image or idea from the book made you feel smallest?”
Then we’ll stay close to the book: Rama, the encounter, the mystery, the scale, the human response, and the strange feeling of meeting something that does not exist to satisfy human curiosity.
Full-book spoilers are expected.
No lore-flexing.
No plot-summary sludge.
No turning the room into a technical manual.
A real science fiction discussion.
